title: Halogen compounds
overview: Extend halogen compound chemistry to more complex mechanisms and reactivity patterns. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.
syllabusPoints: Explain the reactivity difference between halogenoalkanes and halogenoarenes.
Distinguish ring and side-chain halogenation conditions in arenes.
Apply structure and bonding to nucleophilic-substitution predictions.

definitions.definition: A compound with halogen directly bonded to an aromatic-ring carbon.
A compound with halogen bonded to an sp³ carbon of an alkyl group.
A Lewis-acid catalyst such as AlCl₃ or AlBr₃ that helps generate an electrophile.
Bond strengthening caused by overlap/delocalisation that makes a bond shorter and harder to break.
Bond cleavage involving water or aqueous hydroxide.

sections.title: Making halogenoarenes
content: React benzene or methylbenzene with Cl₂/AlCl₃ or Br₂/AlBr₃ to substitute a ring hydrogen. With methylbenzene, the alkyl group directs mainly to 2 and 4 positions. Write HCl or HBr as the other product.
bullets: The catalyst is a halogen carrier, not UV light.
State positional isomers where the directing effect matters.

sections.title: Halogenoarene bonding
content: In chlorobenzene, a chlorine lone pair overlaps with the ring π system, giving the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character. The ring carbon is sp² and the bond is shorter/stronger than in chloroethane, so nucleophilic substitution/hydrolysis is much harder.
bullets: Do not explain the lower reactivity only by bond polarity.
Delocalisation involves a chlorine lone pair and the aromatic system.

sections.title: Ring versus side chain
content: Cl₂/AlCl₃ gives ring substitution; Cl₂ under UV radical conditions attacks an alkyl side chain. The substrate and conditions must both be read before predicting the product.
bullets: A halogen on the side-chain carbon is a halogenoalkane functional group.
A halogen directly on the ring is a halogenoarene.

sections.title: Comparative reaction reasoning
content: Halogenoalkanes can undergo nucleophilic substitution because their polar Cδ⁺–Xδ⁻ bond is accessible and breakable under suitable conditions. Halogenoarenes resist the same conditions because the aromatic carbon–halogen bond is strengthened and the planar electron-rich ring disfavors the usual pathway.
bullets: Compare bond strength, hybridisation/environment and mechanism.
Use named example pairs such as chloroethane/chlorobenzene.

examTips: Draw the bond to the ring explicitly before classifying the compound.
Use a comparison structure: feature in halogenoarene → consequence → lower reactivity.
Use precise chemical vocabulary, balanced equations and stated conditions; link every observation or trend to particles, bonding or equilibrium.
commonMistakes: Using UV light for electrophilic ring substitution.
Explaining chlorobenzene only through a less polar C–Cl bond.

quickRecall.question: Why is chlorobenzene less reactive than chloroethane to nucleophiles?
quickRecall.answer: Its C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character from delocalisation and is shorter/stronger on an sp² carbon.

quickRecall.question: What conditions chlorinate the aromatic ring?
quickRecall.answer: Cl₂ with AlCl₃ as halogen carrier.

quickRecall.question: How is a halogenoarene identified?
quickRecall.answer: The halogen is directly bonded to an aromatic-ring carbon.
